Vibe coding—that is, writing programs via AI prompts—is growing in popularity, and the number of new apps submitted to the App Store has doubled in the first half of 2026, yet downloads have risen by only 2%. Here's the full report.

New app submissions are skyrocketing, but downloads are lagging far behind

The New York Times published a report today, citing the latest data from Sensor Tower, noting that although the number of new apps submitted to the App Store doubled in the first half of 2026, downloads increased by just 2%.

The report also mentioned two developers who have been releasing vibe coding apps on the App Store: Marco Pérez plans to quit his job at JPMorgan next month to work on app development full-time, while David Svensson has launched 11 niche apps over the past five months, treating vibe coding as a hobby rather than a career.

The following are excerpts from the report:

Pérez, a software engineer based in Chicago, had never developed a mobile app before. He spent five weeks in the winter exploring vibe coding AI tools to build a prototype, followed by another two weeks preparing the App Store submission. His app, InfoDrizzle, has performed reasonably well, accumulating 1,300 downloads to date and generating roughly $500 in profit. Pérez's next app proved more popular. He spent about a week launching Stappa in May, a scrapbooking app that turns photos into digital stamps, which has since recorded 20,000 downloads and earned around $3,000 in profit.

Apple spokesperson Peter Ajemian told the New York Times that the surge in submissions has created another problem: as previously reported, the App Store's review process is under enormous strain.

Ajemian pointed out that "Apple has consistently been able to review 90% of app submissions within 48 hours," and added that Apple "welcomes a new generation of developers building and shipping apps at unprecedented speed with the latest tools."

He also stressed that all apps "must meet the same high standards of quality, privacy, and safety that users have always relied on, whether they are developed through vibe coding or not."
